why_angle: The cited pages give total watts and outlet types only. None says how much one 120 V leg can carry when a split-phase inverter runs in 120/240 V mode. That figure is in Honda's manual for the EU7000iS (22.9 A per circuit, so the load must be balanced) and can be worked out from Champion's 37.5 A at 240 V for the 201417 (4,500 W per leg). It decides which unit can run a panel through a transfer switch, and it shows that the most expensive unit has the least per leg.

page.after:
What the differences mean

On a split-phase generator, a 240 V load draws the same current from both legs. So the maker's 240 V running current is also the most one 120 V leg can carry when the 120 V loads are evenly balanced. Where the maker publishes only watts, the per-leg figure below is rated watts ÷ 2.

  • Per-leg power: Champion 201417: 37.5 A × 120 V = 4,500 W. Honda EU7000iS: 22.9 A × 120 V = 2,748 W, which is 61% of the Champion (22.9 ÷ 37.5).
  • Propane: WEN TF1050iX: 8,550 W ÷ 2 = 4,275 W per leg, more than the Champion's 33.7 A × 120 V = 4,044 W on propane.
  • A 32 A Level 2 EV charge: 32 A × 240 V = 7,680 W. The Champion (9,000 W) and the TF1050iX (8,550 W) can hold it. The ecoGen10000 (7,600 W) is 80 W short.
  • Price per continuous 240 V amp: GN875i $899.99 ÷ 29.2 A = $30.8; DF680iX $803.40 ÷ 21.25 A = $37.8; ecoGen10000 $1,299 ÷ 31.7 A = $41.0; TF1050iX $1,649 ÷ 35.6 A = $46.3; Champion $1,999.99 ÷ 37.5 A = $53.3; Honda $4,899 ÷ 22.9 A = $213.9.
  • Gasoline per day at quarter load: Champion 6.08 gal ÷ 15 h × 24 h = 9.7 gal. Honda 5.1 gal ÷ 16 h × 24 h = 7.65 gal.

How a split-phase inverter divides its power between the two legs

Honda's EU7000iS manual explains the mechanism. With the voltage selector in the 120 V/240 V position, 'each set of receptacles is powered by only one power producing circuit that can produce a maximum of 22.9 amps', and 'you must balance the load' between the two sets (receptacles 1, 3 and 4B on one circuit; 2 and 4A on the other). If a refrigerator, a sump pump and a heater all sit on one leg, that leg can trip at about 2,750 W while the generator is still under its 5,500 W rating. The manual's 120 V ONLY position allows 45.8 A total with no balancing, but in that position the 120 V/240 V receptacle must not be used. A house panel that needs 240 V therefore always gets the 22.9 A per-leg limit.

Champion publishes both figures for the 201417: 75 A total at 120 V and 37.5 A at 240 V on gasoline (67.5 A and 33.7 A on propane). That is 37.5 A available on each leg. Champion also rates its 14-50R outlet at 37.5 A, which matches what the engine can supply. Westinghouse sells the ecoGen10000's 14-50R as a '50A outlet', but 7,600 W ÷ 240 V is 31.7 A. Size your transfer switch and breakers to the generator's running current, not to the outlet's rating.

Adding a second unit later. Champion's spec table lists 'Parallel capability: No' for the 201417. Honda says two identical EU7000iS units can be paralleled with an optional kit for up to 14,000 W. WEN's GNA240i kit ($72.69) joins two 240 V WEN inverters through one 50 A, 12,000 W 14-50R outlet. It fits only WEN models with three parallel ports, and the DF680iX manual says its parallel feature works only at 240 V. WEN's similar GNA50i kit puts out 120 V only, so buying it loses split phase. WEN states a bonded neutral on the TF1050iX and DF680iX. Tell your electrician this when choosing the transfer switch or interlock.

Not recommended

Honda EU7000iS for a 120/240 V panel feed. At $4,899 it gives 2,748 W per leg in 120/240 V mode. That is less than the ecoGen10000's roughly 3,800 W at $1,299, and works out to $213.9 per continuous 240 V amp against $53.3 for the Champion 201417. Consumer Reports' lab found it 'handled surges very well' and 'fairly quiet from a distance of 23 feet', so it suits buyers who value low noise over per-leg power. The same Consumer Reports page also notes an August 2023 recall of its fuel filler cap.
